newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Fur dispute issue raised at WTO discussions - Canada.
newsitem.headline: Fur dispute issue raised at WTO discussions - Canada.

text.p: Canada raised the issue of a threatened European Union (EU) ban on most fur imports in trade talks on Tuesday, and expects further discussions on Wednesday, Canadian Trade Minister Art Eggleton said.

"I did raise the matter very briefly, but I'm having a further discussion tomorrow with (EU Trade Commissioner) Leon Brittan about it and hopefully will get a clearer picture at that point of what the next step is," he told reporters.
He was speaking after a series of meetings in conjunction with the World Trade Organisation (WTO) ministerial conference in Singapore, which runs through December 13.

EU environment ministers meeting in Brussels on Monday threatened to impose an import ban on fur from animals caught in leg-hold traps unless negotiators from Canada, Russia and the United States accepted tighter humane trapping standards.

The EU had temporarily suspended a planned ban on imports of fur of species such as muskrats, beavers and sable if they were caught with leg-hold traps, and the ministers instructed the European Commission to take steps to implement the ban by the end of March.

"It wasn't the easiest reception at the environment ministers meeting but there still is another entity that we can go to later in the month, and I will be having discussions with Sir Leon on this tomorrow specifically and hopefully we can get some better understanding of what's likely to happen over the next few weeks," Eggleton said.
In Ottawa on Monday, a Canadian official told reporters Canada would challenge the EU using the WTO dispute resolving mechanism if the EU goes ahead with a ban.
"Without a question Canada would go to the WTO," the official told reporters. "Canada has an extremely strong case and would win."

Canadian officials said the proposed agreement would set improved standards that would be applied not just in Canada, the United States and Russia but also in the EU. They said they were confident a deal would finally be accepted.

But they said that if the ban finally took effect, Canada would use the same argument at the WTO that the EU did in winning a case against the United States on a U.S. ban of tuna caught with nets that also catch dolphins.
In that case, a WTO panel decided that the U.S. restrictions were illegal because the actual tuna did not differ no matter whether it was caught in an environmentally friendly way.
The EU would have that argument turned against it, the Canadian official said, because the actual fur would not differ if leg-hold traps were banned.
